cards.heading: Anatomy of a route
cards.body: Every line in 'show ip route' answers four questions: how the route was learned (the code), which destination prefix it covers, how trustworthy and how good it is [administrative distance/metric], and where to send the packet (next hop or exit interface).
cards.example:
O    172.16.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.0.2, 00:03:11, Gi0/0
│    │              │   │       └ next hop
│    │              │   └ metric (OSPF cost)
│    │              └ administrative distance
│    └ destination prefix
└ code: O = OSPF

cards.heading: Connected and local routes
cards.body: When an interface has an IP address and is up/up, the router adds two routes by itself: C for the connected subnet and L, a /32 for its own address on that interface. Both have administrative distance 0.
cards.example:
C    10.0.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L    10.0.0.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

cards.heading: Longest prefix match
cards.body: To forward a packet the router looks at every route whose prefix contains the destination and uses the most specific one, the longest prefix. AD and metric play no part here; they were already used to decide which routes got into the table.

cards.heading: Administrative distance
cards.body: If two sources offer the same prefix and length, only one is installed: the one with the lowest administrative distance. Metrics are compared only between routes from the same protocol. A floating static route gets a deliberately high AD so it's used only as a backup.
cards.example:
Connected 0   Static 1   eBGP 20   EIGRP 90
OSPF 110      RIP 120    iBGP 200
ip route 10.9.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.0.6 130   ← floating static

cards.heading: The default route
cards.body: 0.0.0.0/0 matches every destination but is the least specific route, so it's used only when nothing else matches. It shows up as the 'gateway of last resort'. With no default route, a packet that matches nothing is dropped.
